reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: Tuberculosis of the spine is the commonest form of skeletal tuberculosis and a major cause of spinal disease in India, typically affecting the lower thoracic and thoracolumbar vertebrae
It usually begins in the anterior vertebral body adjacent to the disc, spreading beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament to involve adjacent vertebrae with relative disc preservation early on
Progressive vertebral destruction and anterior collapse produce a sharp angular kyphosis known as a gibbus deformity
Presentation is insidious with chronic back pain, local tenderness and, in advanced disease, cold paravertebral or psoas abscesses that can track distally
Neurological deficit (Pott's paraplegia) results from cord compression by abscess, granulation tissue, sequestered bone or deformity and is the most feared complication
MRI is the investigation of choice to define the extent, abscesses and cord compression, and tissue sampling confirms the diagnosis and drug susceptibility
Most cases respond to prolonged multidrug anti-tuberculosis therapy, with surgery reserved for significant cord compression, instability, severe deformity or failure of medical treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium tuberculosis reaches the vertebral bodies by haematogenous spread, often via the paravertebral venous plexus, lodging in the well-vascularised anterior vertebral body near the endplate. Granulomatous infection with caseous necrosis destroys bone and later the intervertebral disc, and spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament to contiguous vertebrae. Vertebral collapse causes angular kyphosis, while caseous material and pus form cold abscesses that dissect along tissue planes. Neurological compromise arises from mechanical compression of the cord by abscess, inflammatory tissue, bony sequestra or deformity, and occasionally from vascular compromise of the cord.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the spine to assess bone destruction, abscesses and cord compression
Image-guided biopsy or aspiration for histopathology, molecular testing and culture
Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification for rapid diagnosis and rifampicin resistance
Plain radiography and CT for bony detail and deformity assessment
HIV testing and screening for concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis
redFlags: New or progressive neurological deficit indicating spinal cord compression and requiring urgent evaluation for decompression
Bladder or bowel dysfunction suggesting significant cord or cauda involvement
Spinal instability or severe progressive kyphotic deformity
Large cold abscess with systemic sepsis or rifampicin resistance
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and prolonged multidrug therapy most patients recover well, and even established neurological deficits often improve substantially with treatment and timely surgery; delayed presentation with severe deformity or long-standing cord compression carries a higher risk of permanent disability.
pitfalls: Attributing chronic back pain to mechanical causes and delaying imaging, allowing deformity and deficit to progress
Missing evolving cord compression by not reassessing neurology during treatment
Forgoing tissue diagnosis and drug-susceptibility testing before starting therapy
Confusing it with pyogenic or malignant vertebral disease without confirmatory sampling
management: Prolonged multidrug antituberculous chemotherapy with an intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by an extended continuation phase
Tailor the regimen to drug-susceptibility results, using second-line agents for rifampicin-resistant or multidrug-resistant disease
Spinal immobilisation with bracing and adequate analgesia during healing
Surgical decompression, debridement and instrumented stabilisation for neurological deficit (Pott's paraplegia), spinal instability, progressive kyphosis or a large abscess
Drainage of cold paravertebral or psoas abscesses where indicated
Monitor neurological status, treatment adherence and response, and screen for drug-induced hepatotoxicity
Test for and manage HIV co-infection, screen for concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis, and provide nutritional support
Multidisciplinary care involving spinal surgery, infectious diseases and the tuberculosis service
